questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the deepagents package and create_agent?

options.text: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.
deepagents is a drop-in replacement that fully supersedes create_agent, which vendors now recommend avoiding for new projects.
deepagents and create_agent are unrelated packages maintained by different organizations with no shared foundation or dependency.
create_agent is an internal helper that deepagents exposes only after a project has already adopted the deepagents harness.

questions.explanation: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.

optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-a: deepagents is documented as a separate package that layers additional capabilities on top of create_agent's foundational building blocks, rather than replacing that foundation.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-b: There is no supersession relationship; create_agent remains the recommended choice for lightweight, low-level agent building and is not being phased out in favor of deepagents.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-c: deepagents depends on and builds directly on create_agent's core loop, so the two are not unrelated packages from different organizations with no shared foundation.
optionExplanations.pa-q01-opt-d: create_agent is the standalone, lower-level builder function that exists independently of deepagents; deepagents consumes it as a foundation rather than exposing it only after adoption.

questions.takeaway: deepagents is a separate package built on top of create_agent's core building blocks, not a replacement for it.

questions.stem: A platform team is building their own opinionated agent framework on top of LangChain and wants to assemble every component themselves rather than inherit a pre-built harness. Which builder aligns with that goal?

options.text: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.
deepagents, since its harness exposes every middleware and tool as fully optional, making it functionally equivalent to assembling components individually.
create_agent, since it forces adoption of filesystem tools, skills loading, and sub-agent spawning that cannot be turned off.
deepagents, since it is the only builder that supports customizing the underlying LangGraph runtime for a bespoke framework.

questions.explanation: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.

optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-a: create_agent's minimal defaults and low-level control are exactly suited to a platform team that wants to hand-assemble every component of its own opinionated framework.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-b: deepagents is described as an opinionated harness with capabilities bundled in by default; that is a different design goal from a team wanting to assemble every piece itself from a minimal base.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-c: create_agent does not force adoption of filesystem tools, skills loading, or sub-agent spawning; those are deepagents harness features layered on top, not mandatory parts of create_agent.
optionExplanations.pa-q02-opt-d: Both builders ultimately run on the same LangGraph runtime, and deepagents is not uniquely positioned to customize that runtime for a bespoke framework; create_agent's minimal defaults are what serve this goal.

questions.takeaway: create_agent, since it offers explicit low-level control with minimal defaults for teams that want to define each component themselves.

questions.stem: An agent is configured with two middleware instances, registered in the order `[AuthMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware]`, each implementing both `before_model` and `after_model` hooks. In what order do the `after_model` hooks execute relative to each other?

options.text: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.
`AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, matching their registration order.
Both `after_model` hooks run simultaneously in parallel, since after hooks have no defined ordering guarantee.
Only the last-registered middleware's `after_model` hook runs; earlier middleware hooks are skipped for that phase.

questions.explanation: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.

optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-a: This is correct because after hooks execute in reverse of the middleware registration order, so the last-registered middleware's `after_model` runs first and the first-registered runs last.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-b: This is incorrect because that is the order for `before_model` hooks, which run in registration order; `after_model` hooks run in the opposite, reverse order.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-c: This is incorrect because node-style hooks execute sequentially in a defined order, not concurrently, so there is no race between the two `after_model` calls.
optionExplanations.pa-q03-opt-d: This is incorrect because every registered middleware's `after_model` hook runs on each pass; none are skipped simply because another middleware is also registered.

questions.takeaway: `LoggingMiddleware.after_model` runs, then `AuthMiddleware.after_model` runs, the reverse of their registration order.

questions.stem: A fintech agent handles customer chats that may contain account numbers, executes a `wire_transfer` tool that should require human approval, and must not let a single conversation trigger unlimited transfer attempts. Which middleware components should the team combine to meet all three requirements? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: `PIIMiddleware` configured to detect and redact account-number patterns in conversation messages.
`HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` configured with `interrupt_on` scoped to the `wire_transfer` tool.
`ToolCallLimitMiddleware` scoped to the `wire_transfer` tool with a `thread_limit`.
`ModelFallbackMiddleware` configured with backup models for when the primary provider is unavailable.
`LLMToolEmulator` configured to emulate the `wire_transfer` tool during production traffic.
`TodoListMiddleware` configured to track the agent's task list across the conversation.

questions.explanation: A: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation. | B: Scoping `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`'s `interrupt_on` to the `wire_transfer` tool pauses that specific tool for human approval before it executes. | C: A per-tool `thread_limit` on `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` caps how many times `wire_transfer` can be invoked within a single conversation, preventing unlimited attempts.

optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-a: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-b: Scoping `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`'s `interrupt_on` to the `wire_transfer` tool pauses that specific tool for human approval before it executes.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-c: A per-tool `thread_limit` on `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` caps how many times `wire_transfer` can be invoked within a single conversation, preventing unlimited attempts.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-d: Incorrect — `ModelFallbackMiddleware` addresses model provider outages, not PII protection, approval workflows, or capping tool invocation counts.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-e: Incorrect — `LLMToolEmulator` is meant for testing by replacing real tool execution with simulated responses, which would be unsafe and inappropriate for production wire transfers.
optionExplanations.pa-q04-opt-f: Incorrect — `TodoListMiddleware` equips an agent with task planning and tracking, which does not address PII protection, approvals, or invocation limits.

questions.takeaway: `PIIMiddleware` directly addresses protecting account numbers by detecting and redacting sensitive patterns in the conversation.

questions.stem: A team member creates a new skill directory named `pdf-summarizer` but writes `name: pdf_summarizer` in the SKILL.md frontmatter. At agent startup, the skill fails validation. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.
The `description` field is missing, so the skill can't register regardless of the `name` value that was chosen.
Skill folders require a `scripts/` subdirectory before frontmatter parsing begins, and this skill omitted that required subfolder.
The `allowed-tools` field becomes mandatory whenever a skill's `name` differs from its folder path, and this skill left it out.

questions.explanation: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.

optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-a: The `name` field is defined as a lowercase alphanumeric identifier with hyphens that must exactly match the parent directory name; using an underscore instead of a hyphen produces a mismatch and fails validation.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-b: Nothing in the scenario indicates the `description` field was omitted, so a missing description is not the cause of this particular failure.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-c: There is no requirement that a skill folder contain a `scripts/` subdirectory; supporting folders like scripts, references, and assets are optional additions, not prerequisites for parsing.
optionExplanations.pa-q05-opt-d: There is no rule tying `allowed-tools` to whether `name` matches the folder path; `allowed-tools` is an independent, optional field for pre-approving tool access.

questions.takeaway: The `name` field must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and exactly match the parent directory name, and underscores break that match.

questions.stem: To avoid bloating the system prompt when dozens of skills are configured, only two frontmatter fields are injected into the system prompt for every skill at agent startup, with the rest of each SKILL.md loaded only if that skill is triggered. Which two fields are these?

options.text: `name` and `description`
`name` and `allowed-tools`
`description` and `compatibility`
`name` and `license`

questions.explanation: `name` and `description`

optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-a: Only the `name` and `description` fields are injected into the system prompt for every configured skill at startup, which lets the agent discover skills without paying the token cost of every full body.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-b: `allowed-tools` is not part of the startup metadata injection; it governs which tools a skill may call once it has been activated and its body has been read.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-c: `compatibility` describes environment requirements and is not one of the two fields injected at startup for every skill.
optionExplanations.pa-q06-opt-d: `license` records licensing terms and is not part of the startup metadata; it is only relevant once the full skill body is loaded.

questions.takeaway: `name` and `description`.

questions.stem: In LangChain's context-engineering guidance for long-running agents, what is the key architectural difference between message trimming and the `SummarizationMiddleware` summarization approach?

options.text: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.
Trimming permanently deletes older messages from state entirely, while summarization only hides them briefly during a single isolated model call.
Trimming needs an LLM to condense messages, while summarization discards messages using only token-count heuristics and never a model.
Both approaches persist their changes to state in precisely the same way, differing only in which underlying model actually produces the replacement text.

questions.explanation: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.

optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-a: Trimming is a transient, per-call adjustment that never writes back to state, while summarization is persistent — it replaces older messages in state with a generated summary so future turns see the summary instead of the originals.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-b: Reverses the mechanics: trimming does not touch state at all, and summarization is the one that persists a permanent change, not a temporary one.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-c: Trimming uses simple heuristics like keeping the most recent K messages and requires no LLM call; it is summarization that relies on a model to condense older turns.
optionExplanations.pa-q07-opt-d: Trimming never persists anything to state — only summarization writes a permanent replacement — so the two approaches do not behave identically with respect to state.

questions.takeaway: Trimming drops older messages for one model call without touching state, while summarization permanently overwrites state with a generated summary.

questions.stem: A team debugging a long-running support agent notices that after several summarization cycles, the agent contradicts facts stated at the very start of the conversation, while still performing well on tasks from recent turns. Which explanations are consistent with how `SummarizationMiddleware` operates? (Select 2)

options.text: Once messages fall outside the `keep` window, only the generated summary represents them, so nuanced early details can be lost during condensation.
The summary permanently replaces the original older messages in state, so any information the summarization step dropped is not recoverable from that state.
The middleware re-reads the full original transcript from a separate log on every turn, so summarization cannot cause information loss like this.
Recent messages inside the `keep` window are also condensed into the summary, which is why contradictions appear even in the latest turns.
The summarization model always achieves perfect lossless compression, so any contradiction must come from a prompt or tool bug elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view. | B: Because summarization permanently overwrites state, once information is lost during condensation there is no original copy left in state to recover it from on later turns.

optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-a: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-b: Because summarization permanently overwrites state, once information is lost during condensation there is no original copy left in state to recover it from on later turns.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-c: Incorrect — there is no separate always-consulted transcript log; the middleware relies on the summary once older messages are condensed, so it can indeed lose information this way.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-d: Incorrect — messages inside the `keep` window retain their original form and are not condensed, so contradictions on early facts are not explained by recent-turn messages being summarized.
optionExplanations.pa-q08-opt-e: Incorrect — summarization is lossy by nature since it condenses content through a model, so assuming perfect lossless compression contradicts the observed behavior of losing early details.

questions.takeaway: Details outside the preserved window exist only through the generated summary, so any nuance the summarization step failed to capture is genuinely gone from the model's view.

questions.stem: An agent's sandbox integration is implemented as a subclass that only overrides `execute()`, relying on `BaseSandbox` for everything else, yet the agent still gets working `ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` tools. Which explanation accounts for this?

options.text: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation
Those tools are unrelated to the sandbox subclass and are wired in separately by the model provider
`ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` are implemented as no-op stubs that always return empty results in any sandbox
The subclass must also separately override each filesystem method for them to function, contradicting the premise

questions.explanation: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation.

optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-a: `BaseSandbox` builds the scripts needed for operations like `ls`, `grep`, and `edit_file` and runs them through the single `execute()` method, so a subclass only needs to implement `execute()` for all of these filesystem tools to work.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-b: Incorrect — these filesystem tools are part of the sandbox backend abstraction itself, implemented on top of `execute()`, not something wired in independently by a model provider.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-c: Incorrect — these tools run real generated scripts against the sandbox and return actual results; they are not stub implementations that always return empty output.
optionExplanations.pa-q09-opt-d: Incorrect — `BaseSandbox` deliberately implements filesystem operations on top of a single `execute()` primitive precisely so subclasses do not need to reimplement each filesystem method individually.

questions.takeaway: `BaseSandbox` constructs the scripts for each filesystem operation and runs them through the subclass's `execute()` implementation.

questions.stem: A security review of a sandboxed coding agent concludes that the sandbox successfully stops the agent from touching the host filesystem or host processes. The reviewer still flags a residual risk: a malicious document the agent reads during a task could instruct it to run destructive commands inside the sandbox itself. Why does sandboxing not eliminate this risk?

options.text: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.
Sandboxing only restricts the agent's outbound network traffic and does not filter file contents, so instructions hidden in a document the agent reads are never executed inside the environment.
The `execute()` primitive automatically screens every shell command the agent submits for malicious intent and blocks destructive ones before they run, so poisoned documents cannot cause damage.
Context injection is impossible once a sandbox is configured, because the isolated environment strips untrusted document content before the agent reads it, so the reviewer's concern does not apply.

questions.explanation: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.

optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-a: A sandbox isolates the agent from the host filesystem and host processes, but it does not control what the agent decides to do inside its own environment. A malicious document the agent reads can inject instructions into its context and lead it to issue destructive commands within the sandbox, which is why this residual risk remains.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-b: Incorrect — sandboxing is not limited to restricting outbound network traffic. Its documented scope is filesystem and process isolation from the host. The claim that hidden instructions are never executed inside the environment is also false.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-c: Incorrect — the `execute()` primitive is a generic command-execution method with no built-in screening for malicious intent. It runs whatever command or script it is given and returns the output.
optionExplanations.pa-q10-opt-d: Incorrect — context injection remains possible with a sandbox configured, because the sandbox does not strip or sanitize untrusted document content before the agent reads it. Sandbox outputs should be treated as untrusted and paired with additional controls.

questions.takeaway: Sandboxing isolates the agent from the host system but does not prevent context injection attacks that make the agent issue harmful commands within its own isolated environment.

questions.stem: A platform team is documenting how graphs and deployments relate to each other in Agent Server. Which of the following statements are accurate? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

optionExplanations.pa-q19-opt-b: The same graph's code can serve as the basis for multiple deployments, such as separate staging and production instances, each with its own configuration.

optionExplanations.pa-q19-opt-e: A deployment's revision history tracks its own version number independently of the graph's source code.

questions.stem: Which of the following are recommended practices for handling API keys and tokens used by a deployed LangGraph agent? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: Load credentials from environment variables or a secret management service rather than embedding them in code.
Configure production secrets through the deployment platform's settings so they are scoped per revision.
Commit a `.env` file containing production keys to the repository so the whole team can access it.
Rotate a credential and redeploy whenever there is any indication that the value may have been exposed.
Print credential values to application logs during startup so operators can confirm they loaded correctly.
Paste credential values into chat messages when a teammate needs temporary access for testing.

questions.explanation: A: Loading credentials from environment variables or a secret management service is the core recommended pattern for keeping sensitive values out of source code. | B: Configuring production secrets through deployment platform settings scoped per revision keeps credential changes tracked and applied through a controlled redeploy process. | D: Rotating a credential and redeploying once exposure is suspected limits the window during which a compromised key remains usable.

optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-a: Loading credentials from environment variables or a secret management service is the core recommended pattern for keeping sensitive values out of source code.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-b: Configuring production secrets through deployment platform settings scoped per revision keeps credential changes tracked and applied through a controlled redeploy process.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-c: Committing a `.env` file with production keys exposes those credentials to everyone with repository access and permanently to the commit history.
optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-d: Rotating a credential and redeploying once exposure is suspected limits the window during which a compromised key remains usable.

optionExplanations.pa-q20-opt-f: Pasting credential values into chat messages creates an unmanaged, unauditable copy of the secret outside any access-controlled system.

questions.stem: Which statements about how LangGraph Platform handles secrets across deployment revisions are accurate? (Select all that apply) (Select 3)

options.text: Secrets can be set independently for each revision, so a new revision can introduce or change a credential value.
Rotating a credential typically requires creating a new revision through a redeploy rather than a live in-place edit.
Every revision automatically inherits any change made to a later revision's secrets without additional configuration.
Runs and threads created under an earlier revision continue to reflect the environment that revision was deployed with.
Secret values configured in the deployment settings are stored in plaintext inside the checked-in `langgraph.json`.

questions.explanation: A: Secrets are scoped per revision, so each new revision can introduce a new credential or change an existing one independently of prior revisions. | B: Because secret changes apply to a new revision rather than being live-patched onto a running one, rotating a credential normally requires triggering a redeploy. | D: Runs and threads tied to an earlier revision keep using that revision's environment, which is why an older run can still reflect a since-rotated credential.

optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-a: Secrets are scoped per revision, so each new revision can introduce a new credential or change an existing one independently of prior revisions.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-b: Because secret changes apply to a new revision rather than being live-patched onto a running one, rotating a credential normally requires triggering a redeploy.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-c: Revisions do not automatically inherit later secret changes; each revision keeps the environment it was created with unless it is itself redeployed.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-d: Runs and threads tied to an earlier revision keep using that revision's environment, which is why an older run can still reflect a since-rotated credential.
optionExplanations.pa-q21-opt-e: Secrets configured through deployment settings are managed by the platform separately from `langgraph.json`, not stored in plaintext inside the checked-in configuration file.

questions.stem: A team redeploys their Agent Server, changing `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` from the default endpoint to the EU endpoint so new traffic is served from the EU. What happens to the deployment's existing threads that were created before this change?

options.text: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.
All existing threads are automatically migrated to EU-region PostgreSQL storage as part of the same redeploy operation.
The redeploy is rejected because `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` cannot be changed once a deployment has active threads.
Existing threads become permanently inaccessible the moment the endpoint changes, since revisions do not retain references to prior configurations.

questions.explanation: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.

optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-a: Redeploying with a changed environment variable produces a new revision that governs configuration going forward, but there is no documented step in that process that relocates already-persisted thread data to a different region's storage.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-b: No automatic thread migration between regions is part of a redeploy operation; changing the host URL affects new configuration, not existing persisted data.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-c: Revisions are the standard mechanism for changing a deployment's environment variables and secrets over time, including variables like the host URL.
optionExplanations.pa-q22-opt-d: Existing threads remain in their original backing store and are not described as becoming inaccessible; a revision changes configuration going forward without destroying prior persisted state.

questions.takeaway: A new revision is created with the EU endpoint going forward, but existing threads already persisted under the prior configuration are not relocated by this change alone.

questions.stem: EU-based users report elevated latency when using an agent whose Cloud deployment was created without specifying `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL`. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.
The deployment's queue worker count is too low; adding more workers to the existing region will resolve cross-continental latency regardless of hosting location.
The `LANGSMITH_AUTH_TYPE` variable is misconfigured; switching it to `noop` removes an authentication round-trip that is causing the delay.
The deployment's checkpointer `durability` mode is set to `sync`; switching to `exit` mode reduces network latency for EU requests.

questions.explanation: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.

optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-a: Without explicitly setting `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL`, a Cloud deployment defaults to its standard (non-EU) hosting region, so EU users end up making cross-continental requests; redeploying with the EU endpoint moves the hosting location closer to them.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-b: Adding queue workers increases processing throughput within the deployment's existing region, but it does not shorten the network distance data travels.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-c: `LANGSMITH_AUTH_TYPE` controls how requests are authenticated, not where the deployment's infrastructure is physically located.
optionExplanations.pa-q23-opt-d: The `durability` parameter controls when checkpoint writes are considered persisted during graph execution — a correctness/performance tradeoff unrelated to which region serves EU network requests.

questions.takeaway: The deployment is running on the default (non-EU) endpoint; redeploying with `LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL` set to the EU endpoint routes new traffic through EU-hosted infrastructure.

questions.stem: In the context of a LangSmith Deployment (Agent Server), what is the core conceptual distinction between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.
Authentication decides what a caller may do, while authorization confirms that the caller's credentials are not expired.
Authentication filters which threads a caller can list, while authorization only validates the caller's network origin.
Authentication and authorization both verify identity, differing only in whether the check runs before or after a run completes.

questions.explanation: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.

optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-a: An authentication handler establishes identity on every request, and separate authorization handlers then gate what that identified caller can do to threads, assistants, and crons.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-b: Reverses the roles; permission decisions belong to authorization, while confirming credential validity is part of authentication.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-c: Filtering which threads are visible is an authorization concern handled by resource-level handlers, not a description of authentication.
optionExplanations.pa-q24-opt-d: Authorization does not re-verify identity at all; it consumes the identity already established by authentication and applies permission logic to resources.

questions.takeaway: Authentication confirms who is making a request, while authorization decides what that already-identified caller may do.

questions.stem: Which of the following resources are scoped by returning a metadata filter dictionary (e.g. `{"owner": ctx.user.identity}`) from an `@auth.on` search or list handler? (Select all that apply.) (Select 3)

options.text: Threads
Assistants
Crons
Store
Deployment revisions
Docker build logs

optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-a: Threads are scoped through the standard metadata-filter pattern, where a search or list handler returns a dictionary matched against thread metadata.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-b: Assistants are also scoped through the standard metadata-filter pattern used by resource search and list handlers.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-c: Crons follow the same metadata-filter pattern as threads and assistants for scoping search and list results.
optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-d: The Store resource is authorized differently: its handlers rewrite the mutable `namespace` field to scope access, rather than returning a metadata filter dictionary.

optionExplanations.pa-q25-opt-f: Docker build logs are an infrastructure artifact from the build pipeline and are not a resource type that authorization handlers can scope access to.

questions.stem: During local development a team configures their agent with `durability="sync"` and `InMemorySaver` to test crash recovery. After killing and restarting the process, the thread's prior state is gone. Why?

options.text: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.
`durability="sync"` was configured incorrectly, since sync mode requires `PostgresSaver` to function at all and silently falls back to no persistence.
The thread's `thread_id` was not passed on the restart call, which is the only reason `InMemorySaver` would appear to lose state.
Synchronous checkpoint writes are disabled by default for development builds, so no state was ever written in the first place.

questions.explanation: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.

optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-a: The durability mode only controls the timing of writes relative to graph execution; it does not change where the checkpointer stores data. An in-memory backend never survives a process restart no matter how synchronously it writes.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-b: Sync mode works with any checkpointer implementation, including `InMemorySaver`; it does not require Postgres or silently disable itself when a different backend is used.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-c: Even with the correct `thread_id` supplied, an in-memory backend has nothing to look up after a restart because the underlying process memory holding the checkpoints was cleared.
optionExplanations.pa-q26-opt-d: Durability modes are not disabled based on build type; the checkpoint writes did occur, they simply landed in memory that did not survive the process restart.

questions.takeaway: `InMemorySaver` keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so restarting the process discards them regardless of the durability mode chosen.

questions.stem: What does the checkpointer in LangGraph persist by default, and at what granularity does it write during a run?

options.text: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.
Only the final output message of a run, written as one record once the entire graph execution finishes.
The full conversation across all of a user's threads, written any time any thread belonging to that user changes state.
The graph's static definition and configuration, written once at deployment time rather than during execution.

questions.explanation: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.

optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-a: A checkpointer captures thread-scoped graph state snapshots and writes them at superstep boundaries, which is the core mechanism enabling resumption and fault tolerance.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-b: The checkpointer persists intermediate state throughout the run, not just a final output message, which is what allows recovery from mid-run failures.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-c: This describes the store's cross-thread scope, not the checkpointer, which is deliberately scoped to a single thread.
optionExplanations.pa-q27-opt-d: The graph's code definition is not what the checkpointer persists; it persists runtime execution state, which changes throughout a run.

questions.takeaway: A snapshot of graph state scoped to a thread, written at superstep boundaries as nodes complete their scheduled work.

Make the discovery description specify invoice reconciliation and its trigger conditions.
Increase model output-token limits without improving discovery metadata.
Add the complete skill body to every prompt regardless of task relevance.

questions.explanation: The discovery description helps the model decide when a skill is relevant before reading its body. Better trigger wording is more targeted than loading every skill into context.
questions.takeaway: The discovery description helps the model decide when a skill is relevant before reading its body. Better trigger wording is more targeted than loading every skill into context.

questions.stem: A sandbox contains a production API key and permits outbound requests to the service using that key. Which risks remain? Select 2.

options.text: Code inside the sandbox may use the key to perform externally authorized actions.
Sandboxing turns every remote API key into a read-only credential.
A sandbox boundary does not by itself restrict the credential's remote permissions.
Host filesystem isolation guarantees that no network action can occur.

questions.explanation: Sandbox isolation and remote credential privileges are separate boundaries. Credentials and egress must be scoped to the task; isolation alone cannot revoke permissions at an external service.
questions.takeaway: Sandbox isolation and remote credential privileges are separate boundaries. Credentials and egress must be scoped to the task; isolation alone cannot revoke permissions at an external service.

questions.topic: 1.1 create_agent and Deep Agents harness choices
questions.stem: A specialist produces 150 pages of intermediate findings. Its parent needs a two-paragraph conclusion and may later inspect the full findings. Which handoff best uses the Deep Agents harness?

options.text: Have the parent perform all research steps in its own conversation and summarize at the end.
Return the full report and rely on parent summarization to discard unnecessary detail later.
Write findings to an accessible backend path and return a concise conclusion plus that path.
Return only the conclusion and discard the report even though later inspection is required.

questions.explanation: A file artifact preserves detail while a concise return protects parent context. Accessibility depends on backend routing and permissions. Returning all intermediate data defeats that context-management goal.
questions.takeaway: A file artifact preserves detail while a concise return protects parent context. Accessibility depends on backend routing and permissions. Returning all intermediate data defeats that context-management goal.

questions.stem: A review interrupt offers only approve and reject for send_email. The reviewer must correct a recipient before execution. Which configuration change directly enables that workflow?

options.text: Include edit in that tool's allowed_decisions and implement the corresponding resume decision.
Keep approve/reject only and modify the proposed arguments after the tool executes.
Use a model-fallback configuration so a second model can bypass the missing review decision.
Change the proposed call solely in the monitoring trace, then approve the original interruption.

questions.explanation: An edit decision changes the proposed action before it executes. Trace edits after approval do not correct a sent email; monitoring configuration does not modify HITL decisions.
questions.takeaway: An edit decision changes the proposed action before it executes. Trace edits after approval do not correct a sent email; monitoring configuration does not modify HITL decisions.

questions.stem: An agent stores draft files in StateBackend and user preferences in StoreBackend through separate routes. Which results are expected? Select 2.

options.text: Drafts can remain available on later turns of the same checkpointed thread.
The store makes every file part of the model prompt on every call.
Preferences can be retrieved in another thread if the persistent store and namespace permit it.
Every StateBackend file is automatically visible in every user's threads.

questions.explanation: Backend scope controls persistence and sharing. Thread state and cross-thread store data serve different purposes; stored data is not automatically fully inserted into every model prompt.
questions.takeaway: Backend scope controls persistence and sharing. Thread state and cross-thread store data serve different purposes; stored data is not automatically fully inserted into every model prompt.

questions.stem: A developer grants skill A access only to readonly reporting tools in prose, but also binds a write-capable custom tool to the agent. Which statements are correct? Select 2.

options.text: Any word readonly in a skill automatically disables all mutating tools.
Reading a skill does not make its prose an enforceable service-side permission boundary.
A skill's description is the authenticated user identity.
Skill instructions should be backed by actual tool and service permissions.

questions.explanation: Procedural instructions and enforced permissions are different layers. Restrict tool availability where appropriate and enforce authorization in the implementation. Descriptive text does not establish caller identity.
questions.takeaway: Procedural instructions and enforced permissions are different layers. Restrict tool availability where appropriate and enforce authorization in the implementation. Descriptive text does not establish caller identity.

questions.stem: A sandbox prevents access to host processes. An agent nevertheless deletes its only in-sandbox report before returning. Which additional design most directly addresses this loss?

options.text: Persist only the conversation text and expect it to contain the deleted file's complete contents.
Preserve important outputs in separate durable storage and control destructive operations.
Assume host-process isolation also guarantees that every in-sandbox output is retained.
Use a fresh sandbox after deletion and assume the earlier filesystem is automatically cloned.

questions.explanation: Isolation protects an execution boundary; it does not guarantee artifact retention. Durable output handling and destructive-operation controls address this specific failure mode.
questions.takeaway: Isolation protects an execution boundary; it does not guarantee artifact retention. Durable output handling and destructive-operation controls address this specific failure mode.

questions.topic: 1.1 create_agent and Deep Agents harness choices
questions.stem: A specialized subagent should use a smaller model without changing the parent model or rebuilding the whole application. Which configuration is most direct?

options.text: Set the model override on that subagent definition.
Change only the specialist prompt to name the desired model, without setting its model override.
Select an assistant name for the specialist but leave its model configuration unchanged.
Set only the parent model and assume the specialist keeps an independently chosen default.

questions.explanation: Subagents support their own model overrides. Thread identifiers and tool names do not select a model. Changing the parent model is broader than the stated requirement.
questions.takeaway: Subagents support their own model overrides. Thread identifiers and tool names do not select a model. Changing the parent model is broader than the stated requirement.

questions.stem: An agent must use a cheaper model for short conversations and a stronger model after the history grows. Which hook is best suited to selecting the model for the current call?

options.text: wrap_tool_call, changing the tool return value instead of the pending model request.
wrap_model_call, invoking the handler with a request whose model is overridden.
Set a fixed model once at construction, leaving it unchanged as history grows.
after_model, replacing the model after that call has already generated its response.

questions.explanation: Model-call wrapping can inspect the request and select a model before execution. Tool wrappers operate on tool calls, and tracing tags describe execution rather than changing it.
questions.takeaway: Model-call wrapping can inspect the request and select a model before execution. Tool wrappers operate on tool calls, and tracing tags describe execution rather than changing it.

questions.stem: A summarized conversation must retain the exact, authoritative purchase order number for later actions. Which design best reduces the risk of lossy compression changing it?

options.text: Keep the validated identifier in structured state or durable storage and retrieve it when needed.
Keep the identifier solely in the summary and assume an exact-retention instruction is lossless.
Use the model's most recent generated identifier as the authoritative value without validation.
Retain the identifier only in old messages that are removed after summarization.

questions.explanation: Authoritative fields should have an explicit source of truth outside lossy narrative compression. A summarization instruction does not guarantee exact retention; older removed messages may no longer be available.
questions.takeaway: Authoritative fields should have an explicit source of truth outside lossy narrative compression. A summarization instruction does not guarantee exact retention; older removed messages may no longer be available.

questions.stem: Only premium accounts should discover a private analysis skill. The application already has trusted account context. What should drive the skill list?

options.text: A runtime selection function that returns allowed skill paths based on that trusted context.
Accept the role stated in the user message as the runtime source of truth.
Use a shared skill list selected once for the first user of the process.
Expose every skill but tell the model to ignore private ones for non-premium users.

questions.explanation: Dynamic skill availability can use runtime context. It should use verified account facts rather than self-asserted chat content or unrelated evaluation signals.
questions.takeaway: Dynamic skill availability can use runtime context. It should use verified account facts rather than self-asserted chat content or unrelated evaluation signals.

questions.stem: Each agent turn creates a fresh sandbox, but the conversation expects files written on earlier turns to remain. What must the application arrange?

options.text: Regenerate filenames on each turn and assume the original file contents become available.
Checkpoint conversation messages and assume unrelated external files are stored in those messages.
Reuse only the same thread ID while discarding every external sandbox after each turn.
Reuse the appropriate sandbox or explicitly persist and restore required artifacts.

questions.explanation: Conversation checkpoints do not automatically preserve every external execution environment. Sandbox lifecycle and artifact persistence must align with the desired conversation lifecycle.
questions.takeaway: Conversation checkpoints do not automatically preserve every external execution environment. Sandbox lifecycle and artifact persistence must align with the desired conversation lifecycle.

questions.stem: An agent uses the correct tools but reports the wrong account balance. What should an evaluation suite reveal?

options.text: One latency metric can substitute for both quality criteria.
Correct tool selection proves final-answer correctness.
Trajectory success can coexist with final-answer failure, so evaluate both criteria.
A failed answer proves the tool trajectory was necessarily wrong.

questions.explanation: Tool trajectory and final output measure different properties. Correct intermediate actions do not guarantee faithful synthesis, and latency does not measure answer correctness.
questions.takeaway: Tool trajectory and final output measure different properties. Correct intermediate actions do not guarantee faithful synthesis, and latency does not measure answer correctness.

questions.stem: An online evaluator runs only on traces with thumbs-down feedback. Its pass rate is 35%. Which interpretation is warranted?

options.text: It describes the evaluated, negatively selected subset, not necessarily all production traffic.
Treat the thumbs-down filter as equivalent to a random sample of all traffic.
Report it as a 65% failure rate across all production requests.
Compare it directly with an offline pass rate on a different happy-path population.

questions.explanation: Filtering changes the evaluated population. A deliberately selected subset is useful for diagnosis but cannot automatically estimate full-population quality or support unmatched comparisons.
questions.takeaway: Filtering changes the evaluated population. A deliberately selected subset is useful for diagnosis but cannot automatically estimate full-population quality or support unmatched comparisons.

questions.stem: An experiment has a common slice with 90 examples and 90% accuracy, and a rare slice with 10 examples and 20% accuracy. What is the overall example-weighted accuracy?
questions.explanation: The slices contribute 81 and 2 correct answers, giving 83/100. An unweighted average of the two slice percentages is 55% and measures a different quantity.
questions.takeaway: The slices contribute 81 and 2 correct answers, giving 83/100. An unweighted average of the two slice percentages is 55% and measures a different quantity.

questions.stem: Two domain experts disagree on whether a borderline refund response violates policy. What should the team address before tuning the judge toward one label?

options.text: Pick one reviewer's label arbitrarily and optimize agreement with it.
Add both contradictory labels as few-shot examples without clarifying the rubric.
Clarify the rubric and adjudicate the disputed human label.
Use the judge's majority prediction to decide the human policy label automatically.

questions.explanation: Ambiguous human standards create ambiguous alignment targets. Clarify the policy and labeling instructions first; model scores, concurrency, and dataset versioning do not resolve the underlying judgment.
questions.takeaway: Ambiguous human standards create ambiguous alignment targets. Clarify the policy and labeling instructions first; model scores, concurrency, and dataset versioning do not resolve the underlying judgment.

questions.stem: A regression dataset is expanded with reviewed examples of an outage pattern. Which practices preserve useful comparisons? Select 2.

options.text: Keep the old version available for matched historical comparisons.
Overwrite all old outputs with the candidate's answers.
Remove every previously passing example to guarantee a lower score.
Evaluate the candidate on the new failure slice as well as the broader dataset.

questions.explanation: Version history preserves a comparison baseline, while slice evaluation targets newly discovered failures. Replacing references with candidate answers or discarding coverage distorts measurement.
questions.takeaway: Version history preserves a comparison baseline, while slice evaluation targets newly discovered failures. Replacing references with candidate answers or discarding coverage distorts measurement.

questions.stem: A classifier needs one F1 score from all predictions and labels in an experiment. Which design choices fit? Select 2.

options.text: Use a summary evaluator for the experiment-wide metric.
Use only the longest response from the experiment.
Use an online rule on one production trace instead of the experiment outputs.
Compute aggregate true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative counts across the examples.
Compute a score for each example independently and assume its average must equal dataset F1.

questions.explanation: F1 depends on aggregate true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative counts. Summary evaluators support experiment-wide metrics; averaging arbitrary single-example F1 values need not reproduce dataset F1.
questions.takeaway: F1 depends on aggregate true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative counts. Summary evaluators support experiment-wide metrics; averaging arbitrary single-example F1 values need not reproduce dataset F1.

questions.stem: A team wants to apply a newly written Python evaluator to last week's saved experiment outputs without calling the application model again. What should it do?

options.text: Pass the existing experiment name or ID to evaluate or aevaluate with the new evaluator.
Use an online alert threshold instead of actually running the new evaluation metric.
Pass the target function again and assume earlier predictions are reused automatically.
Recreate all target outputs with the new application version, then label them as last week's outputs.

questions.explanation: The Python SDK can evaluate cached traces from an existing experiment. Supplying a target function instead requests application execution; scoring old outputs still incurs any judge costs.
questions.takeaway: The Python SDK can evaluate cached traces from an existing experiment. Supplying a target function instead requests application execution; scoring old outputs still incurs any judge costs.

questions.stem: Experiment A used 50 old dataset examples. Experiment B used the latest version, including 30 added difficult examples. B scores lower. What should happen before attributing the change to the prompt?

options.text: Compare both variants on the same pinned dataset version and scoring setup.
Treat the dataset name as sufficient proof that both experiments used identical examples.
Compare the two raw percentages without accounting for the different examples.
Remove the newly added hard cases only from B so its rate resembles A's rate.

questions.explanation: Different datasets confound the comparison. A matched version and scoring setup isolates the candidate change; removing difficult cases to improve a score distorts the test.
questions.takeaway: Different datasets confound the comparison. A matched version and scoring setup isolates the candidate change; removing difficult cases to improve a score distorts the test.

questions.stem: Human labels contain 95 passes and 5 important failures. A judge predicts pass for all 100 and reports 95% agreement. What is the strongest next check?

options.text: Accept the judge because agreement above 90% proves adequate failure detection.
Inspect failure-class recall and disagreement cases; overall agreement hides all five missed failures.
Replace human labels with the judge labels to remove disagreements.
Delete the five failures to achieve complete agreement.

questions.explanation: An imbalanced label set can make a useless always-pass judge look aligned. It misses every failure here. Class-level metrics and disagreement review reveal the weakness.
questions.takeaway: An imbalanced label set can make a useless always-pass judge look aligned. It misses every failure here. Class-level metrics and disagreement review reveal the weakness.

questions.stem: A production trace with an incorrect answer is converted into a dataset example. What should become the reference answer?

options.text: Copy the candidate's next response into the reference so it always matches.
A reviewed correct answer or appropriate reviewed acceptance criteria.
Leave the reference labeled correct because the trace completed without a runtime exception.
Use the failed production output as the reference without human review.

questions.explanation: A trace supplies realistic inputs and observed behavior, but its output may be wrong. Review references or acceptance criteria before using them as an evaluation target.
questions.takeaway: A trace supplies realistic inputs and observed behavior, but its output may be wrong. Review references or acceptance criteria before using them as an evaluation target.

questions.stem: An offline dataset contains inputs but no reference answers. The team wants to check whether each output parses as valid JSON. What is correct?

options.text: JSON validity can be judged only by comparing two experiments.
Every offline evaluator is invalid unless references exist.
A reference-free code evaluator can perform the check on the target outputs.
Adding a thread ID manufactures the missing reference answers.

questions.explanation: Dataset reference outputs are optional for reference-free criteria. JSON parsing does not need a gold answer. Whether references are required depends on the evaluator.
questions.takeaway: Dataset reference outputs are optional for reference-free criteria. JSON parsing does not need a gold answer. Whether references are required depends on the evaluator.

questions.stem: A refund agent is evaluated on a dataset in a staging environment. Which precautions support a valid test? Select 2.

options.text: Keep the business decision logic being tested representative of the intended application.
Replace every tool result with success and claim end-to-end policy correctness.
Use controlled test data and prevent unintended real refund side effects.
Use production payment credentials so every evaluation refund is real.

questions.explanation: Evaluation needs controlled side effects while exercising relevant logic. Blindly successful stubs can hide decision errors; real financial actions are unnecessary to validate dataset behavior.
questions.takeaway: Evaluation needs controlled side effects while exercising relevant logic. Blindly successful stubs can hide decision errors; real financial actions are unnecessary to validate dataset behavior.

questions.stem: Both variants ran on the same 100 examples. Results: both pass=78; A-only pass=8; B-only pass=6; both fail=8. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A passes 86 and B passes 84, while B introduces 8 regressions and fixes 6 A failures.
B has no regressions because its total pass rate exceeds 80%.
A passes 78 and B passes 78 because only shared successes count.
A's advantage proves statistical significance without further assumptions.

questions.explanation: Totals are shared passes plus variant-only passes. Moving A→B loses eight previously passing cases and gains six. Aggregate improvement and statistical significance require more analysis than totals alone.
questions.takeaway: Totals are shared passes plus variant-only passes. Moving A→B loses eight previously passing cases and gains six. Aggregate improvement and statistical significance require more analysis than totals alone.

questions.stem: A judge prompt is repeatedly tuned on the same 20 human-labeled examples and reaches 100% agreement. Which validation practices are appropriate before production? Select 2.

options.text: Evaluate only exact copies of the examples inserted into the few-shot prompt.
Check agreement on a separate representative labeled set not used for tuning.
Report tuning-set agreement as proof of generalization.
Review the held-out disagreements against the rubric rather than silently replacing human labels.
Use the judge's predictions as the new independent human labels.

questions.explanation: Held-out labeled cases test generalization beyond tuned examples. Review disagreements against the intended rubric; model-generated labels and demonstration-set agreement are not independent validation.
questions.takeaway: Held-out labeled cases test generalization beyond tuned examples. Review disagreements against the intended rubric; model-generated labels and demonstration-set agreement are not independent validation.

questions.stem: CI reads a dataset version using the tag release. That tag is later moved to a newer version. What is needed to reproduce the earlier run exactly?

options.text: Record the resolved dataset version timestamp or equivalent immutable version identity from the earlier run.
Record only release and assume the tag can never reference a different version.
Record only the dataset display name and the aggregate score.
Use the latest version and increase repetitions until its score resembles the earlier run.

questions.explanation: A human-readable tag can identify a version at a point in time; reproducibility should record the resolved version rather than assume a mutable name always refers to the same data.
questions.takeaway: A human-readable tag can identify a version at a point in time; reproducibility should record the resolved version rather than assume a mutable name always refers to the same data.

questions.stem: An evaluator reads outputs["answer"], but the target returns {"response": "Approved"}. Every row reports an evaluator exception. What is the best first action?

options.text: Classify evaluator exceptions as measured application failures without checking the error.
Increase num_repetitions while leaving the incompatible output key unchanged.
Align the evaluator and target output schemas before interpreting quality scores.
Tune a judge rubric even though the error occurs before the intended criterion is evaluated.

questions.explanation: A schema mismatch breaks evaluation before the intended criterion is assessed. Evaluator infrastructure errors should be diagnosed separately from application-quality failures. Repetition cannot supply a missing field.
questions.takeaway: A schema mismatch breaks evaluation before the intended criterion is assessed. Evaluator infrastructure errors should be diagnosed separately from application-quality failures. Repetition cannot supply a missing field.

questions.stem: A new model must be tested against historical customer requests before it receives live traffic. Which workflow fits?

options.text: Replay only previously successful requests and generalize the result to all customer cases.
Compare model specifications and skip execution on historical requests.
Run an online evaluator on the old model and treat its outputs as the new model's benchmark.
Create a curated dataset from historical requests and run an offline backtest of the new model.

questions.explanation: Backtesting runs a candidate on historical inputs. Scoring the old model does not execute the candidate, and product specifications do not establish task performance.
questions.takeaway: Backtesting runs a candidate on historical inputs. Scoring the old model does not execute the candidate, and product specifications do not establish task performance.

questions.stem: A Python experiment has 24 dataset examples and num_repetitions=3. All target calls complete. How many target predictions are expected, excluding evaluator calls?
questions.explanation: Each example is evaluated three times: 24 × 3 = 72 target predictions. Evaluator calls are separate and may further increase workload and cost.
questions.takeaway: Each example is evaluated three times: 24 × 3 = 72 target predictions. Evaluator calls are separate and may further increase workload and cost.

questions.stem: A judge matches human labels on 42 of 50 reviewed cases. Under a simple agreement definition, what is its alignment percentage?
questions.explanation: Agreement is 42/50 = 0.84. This is agreement with the supplied human labels, not an independent proof that the application is correct on 84% of all traffic.
questions.takeaway: Agreement is 42/50 = 0.84. This is agreement with the supplied human labels, not an independent proof that the application is correct on 84% of all traffic.

questions.stem: A vision agent is evaluated on image descriptions, but the dataset stores only filenames from a developer's laptop. What must be verified?

options.text: Adding a human-readable dataset tag uploads all local images.
The target and evaluator can access the actual image content or attachments in the evaluation environment.
A text-only exact-match evaluator reconstructs images from their names.
A filename alone gives the remote judge the image pixels.

questions.explanation: Multimodal evaluation needs the underlying content, not just an inaccessible local path. Confirm attachment and input mapping for both the application and evaluator.
questions.takeaway: Multimodal evaluation needs the underlying content, not just an inaccessible local path. Confirm attachment and input mapping for both the application and evaluator.

questions.stem: A policy response must have the required JSON schema and must explain a refusal respectfully. Which assessment best separates the criteria? Select 2.

options.text: Use deterministic validation for the required structure.
Treat valid JSON as proof that the refusal is respectful.
Use response length as the sole measure of policy correctness.
Use an aligned rubric-based judge or human review for the respectful explanation.

questions.explanation: Structural validity and semantic quality are different criteria. A response can pass one and fail the other. Schema checks and a validated qualitative rubric provide complementary evidence.
questions.takeaway: Structural validity and semantic quality are different criteria. A response can pass one and fail the other. Schema checks and a validated qualitative rubric provide complementary evidence.

questions.stem: An evaluator rule is created with a backfill over past runs. Immediately afterward no scores are visible. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat missing scores as zero-quality results before checking background execution.
Check evaluator logs and background-job progress before concluding that the rule failed.
Assume backfill is synchronous and recreate the rule immediately because scores are absent.
Wait for new traffic only and assume past runs cannot be evaluated.

questions.explanation: Backfill is processed in the background and results are not immediate. Logs help distinguish ongoing processing from failures. Fabricating scores or changing graph deployment does not verify evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Backfill is processed in the background and results are not immediate. Logs help distinguish ongoing processing from failures. Fabricating scores or changing graph deployment does not verify evaluation.

questions.stem: An evaluation job hits provider rate limits. The team wants fewer simultaneous requests while keeping the same examples and repetitions. Which setting is the most direct control?

options.text: Reduce num_repetitions even though prediction count must stay the same.
Change only experiment_prefix so the provider treats requests as unrelated.
Reduce max_concurrency.
Increase max_concurrency to complete requests before the provider sees rate limits.

questions.explanation: max_concurrency controls parallel work. Repetitions affect prediction count, not the desired concurrency limit; an experiment name is only descriptive. Actual request limits may also require retry and pacing policies.
questions.takeaway: max_concurrency controls parallel work. Repetitions affect prediction count, not the desired concurrency limit; an experiment name is only descriptive. Actual request limits may also require retry and pacing policies.

questions.stem: A pairwise judge tends to prefer whichever output appears first. Which intervention directly targets this bias?

options.text: Run more comparisons with fixed order and assume repetition eliminates positional bias.
Compare response length instead of the required quality criterion.
Always place the candidate believed to be better first.
Randomize presentation order and review the judge prompt for positional bias.

questions.explanation: Order randomization helps mitigate positional bias, alongside rubric and prompt improvements. Always presenting one candidate first preserves the confound. Output length and resource IDs do not address it.
questions.takeaway: Order randomization helps mitigate positional bias, alongside rubric and prompt improvements. Always presenting one candidate first preserves the confound. Output length and resource IDs do not address it.

questions.stem: The evaluation target expects {"question": string}, but a CSV import produces examples with only {"prompt": string}. What should the importer or target adapter do?

options.text: Move prompt to reference outputs and omit the required application input.
Rename the dataset but leave the incompatible field mapping unchanged.
Map the imported field to the target's expected input schema.
Change the judge model while leaving the target input adapter unchanged.

questions.explanation: Dataset inputs must match the target function or be explicitly adapted. Reference outputs and judge selection do not transform incompatible application input fields.
questions.takeaway: Dataset inputs must match the target function or be explicitly adapted. Reference outputs and judge selection do not transform incompatible application input fields.

questions.stem: A tool-use evaluator requires lookup_order before refund_order but allows an additional harmless read between them. What should it check?

options.text: That the required calls occur in the required relative order, with any explicit forbidden-call checks separately.
Check exact equality with the two required calls, rejecting every additional harmless read.
Check only membership of the two tool names, without relative ordering.
Grade only the final answer against a reference and assume it establishes the tool sequence.

questions.explanation: An ordered-subsequence criterion matches the stated allowance. Exact matching is stricter; set matching ignores ordering; final-answer grading misses the execution requirement.
questions.takeaway: An ordered-subsequence criterion matches the stated allowance. Exact matching is stricter; set matching ignores ordering; final-answer grading misses the execution requirement.

questions.stem: A reference-based offline correctness judge is moved unchanged to production. It requires reference_outputs["answer"], but production traces have no references. What should change?

options.text: Use the actual output as its own reference answer.
Use a reference-free production criterion or supply an explicit appropriate reference source.
Interpret missing references as a passing correctness result.
Assume LangSmith generates authoritative references for every production request.

questions.explanation: A reference-dependent judge cannot compare against unavailable labels. Actual outputs are not independent ground truth; missing evidence does not establish correctness.
questions.takeaway: A reference-dependent judge cannot compare against unavailable labels. Actual outputs are not independent ground truth; missing evidence does not establish correctness.

questions.stem: Quality rose from 0.84 to 0.88 after both the application prompt and judge rubric changed. Which conclusions are justified? Select 2.

options.text: The numbers alone do not isolate the application prompt's effect.
Rescoring comparable outputs under a common rubric can help separate scoring changes from application changes.
A different judge rubric cannot affect reported quality.
The 0.04 difference proves that every previously failed example now passes.

questions.explanation: Changing the measurement and the application simultaneously confounds the outcome. Common-rubric comparison helps; an aggregate score does not identify which individual examples improved.
questions.takeaway: Changing the measurement and the application simultaneously confounds the outcome. Common-rubric comparison helps; an aggregate score does not identify which individual examples improved.

questions.stem: A judge is meant to verify that a risky tool was never called. Its mapped variables contain only the final answer. Which problem should be fixed first?

options.text: Increase the score threshold without changing the evidence supplied to the judge.
Provide the execution evidence needed by the criterion, such as logged trajectory or relevant child runs.
Change only the rubric wording while keeping execution evidence unavailable.
Use final-answer tone as a proxy for whether the risky tool was executed.

questions.explanation: A judge cannot reliably assess unseen actions. Input mapping must expose relevant trace evidence; wording and thresholds cannot replace missing information.
questions.takeaway: A judge cannot reliably assess unseen actions. Input mapping must expose relevant trace evidence; wording and thresholds cannot replace missing information.

questions.stem: Turns from the same conversation are randomly divided between a tuning set and a final evaluation set. Why is this problematic?

options.text: LangSmith disables every dataset that contains multiple turns.
Reference outputs become mandatory for all reference-free evaluators.
Shared conversation content can leak information across the two sets; partitioning by conversation reduces that risk.
Every conversation must belong to the monitoring project instead of a dataset.

questions.explanation: Related conversation turns are not independent examples for leakage-sensitive validation. Grouped partitioning is a methodology choice; multi-turn datasets themselves remain useful.
questions.takeaway: Related conversation turns are not independent examples for leakage-sensitive validation. Grouped partitioning is a methodology choice; multi-turn datasets themselves remain useful.

questions.stem: One conversation thread has four sequential agent invocations. Which resource accounting best describes this?

options.text: One run, because a thread is a single execution rather than a sequence of executions.
One thread containing four runs, with state accumulated according to graph logic.
Four assistant configurations, because each run must create a new assistant.
Four threads, because each invocation automatically requires a separate conversation container.

questions.explanation: A thread can contain a sequence of runs. Conversation continuity does not require a new deployment or revision for each invocation.
questions.takeaway: A thread can contain a sequence of runs. Conversation continuity does not require a new deployment or revision for each invocation.

questions.stem: A hybrid deployment uses a LangSmith control plane while Agent Servers and databases run in the team's infrastructure. Which placement matters most for where graph execution and checkpoint storage occur?

options.text: The developer workstation's location, because Studio is the execution data plane.
The region of the LangSmith control-plane dashboard alone, regardless of self-hosted server placement.
The model provider's region alone, regardless of where checkpoints are stored.
The data-plane infrastructure where the Agent Servers and databases actually run.

questions.explanation: The data plane hosts Agent Servers and supporting persistence. The control plane manages desired deployment state; the dashboard address alone does not establish where self-hosted execution occurs.
questions.takeaway: The data plane hosts Agent Servers and supporting persistence. The control plane manages desired deployment state; the dashboard address alone does not establish where self-hosted execution occurs.

questions.stem: A leaked credential has been replaced in the deployment, but the old credential remains valid at its issuer. What issue remains?

options.text: Assume updating the deployment environment automatically revokes the issuer's old key.
Rotate a key on a different provider account and assume it invalidates the exposed credential.
Delete only local copies and assume an already leaked key becomes unusable.
Anyone holding the old credential may still use it until it is revoked or otherwise invalidated.

questions.explanation: Updating application configuration and revoking a credential are separate actions. An exposed credential remains usable according to the issuing service's rules until invalidated.
questions.takeaway: Updating application configuration and revoking a credential are separate actions. An exposed credential remains usable according to the issuing service's rules until invalidated.

questions.stem: A privacy test confirms Alice cannot list Bob's thread, but Alice can fetch it directly when given its ID. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Treat knowledge of a thread ID as sufficient permission to access the thread.
Retest only token validity, because a valid identity must permit every read.
Treat a filtered search result as proof that direct reads are also protected.
Authorization must cover direct reads and other relevant operations, not just search results.

questions.explanation: Restricting lists is insufficient if direct resource access bypasses policy. Resource authorization needs consistent operation coverage, including direct read and mutation paths.
questions.takeaway: Restricting lists is insufficient if direct resource access bypasses policy. Resource authorization needs consistent operation coverage, including direct read and mutation paths.

questions.stem: A user opens a new conversation but should retain account preferences without inheriting the old conversation messages. Which arrangement fits?

options.text: Store preferences only in the old thread and assume every new thread loads them.
Create a new deployment whenever the user starts a conversation.
Use a new thread for conversation state and a persistent user-scoped store for preferences.
Reuse every user's single global thread so all preferences remain visible.

questions.explanation: Thread state and cross-thread memory have different scopes. A new thread can isolate the conversation while a user-scoped persistent store supplies durable preferences.
questions.takeaway: Thread state and cross-thread memory have different scopes. A new thread can isolate the conversation while a user-scoped persistent store supplies durable preferences.

questions.stem: Two assistants use one deployed graph with different model_name context values, and the graph reads that field. Which statements are accurate? Select 2.

options.text: These assistant configurations can share the same deployed graph infrastructure.
Creating each assistant necessarily rewrites the graph source.
Each assistant is itself the accumulated state of one user conversation.
Assistant context can select different behavior supported by the shared graph code.
Context values affect model choice even if the graph ignores them.

questions.explanation: Assistants configure a deployed graph. Their values affect behavior only where the graph uses them; assistants are not themselves separate deployments or conversation containers.
questions.takeaway: Assistants configure a deployed graph. Their values affect behavior only where the graph uses them; assistants are not themselves separate deployments or conversation containers.

questions.stem: A Cloud deployment and its database must move to another data region. What does current deployment documentation imply?

options.text: Edit LANGGRAPH_HOST_URL and all checkpoints move immediately.
Creating a new assistant on the same deployment changes its database region.
Changing the model provider name moves every server resource.
Plan a deployment in the target-region organization and an explicit supported data-transition strategy; existing deployments are not region-migrated automatically.

questions.explanation: Current Cloud documentation ties deployment data region to the organization and states that deployments and underlying databases cannot migrate between regions. Do not assume environment edits copy persistent state.
